children: By Sarah Paynter

In August 2014, cannon fire rang out across Richard van Stolk's family farm in Chestertown, Md., setting off car alarms and startling the neighbors. They would have to put up with the noise: History buffs were practicing for the re-enactment of the Battle of Caulk's Field, says local historian Kevin Hemstock, who helped organize the 200-year anniversary event.
For two centuries, bullets, buttons, buckles, thimbles and coins lay buried in Maryland's best-preserved battlefield from the War of 1812, according to a report from the National Park Service.
Archaeologists reconstructed the battle using the locations of 721 artifacts, the report says. After years of preparation, some 5,000 spectators watched men in wool uniforms act out the battle.
The history

According to the 1998 book "Historic Houses of Kent County," farmer William Moore built a brick house on the property in 1743. His grandson, farmer Isaac Caulk, inherited it in 1812. Two years later, the farm became a battlefield.

American militia forces set up camp on the farm. On Aug. 31, 1814, shortly after the British burned Washington, D.C., they confronted enemy troops during the Battle of Caulk's Field. Fourteen British soldiers were killed-including captain Peter Parker of the Royal Navy-and 27 others were wounded. The resulting British retreat boosted American morale before their pivotal comeback at the Battle of Baltimore in mid-September, according to the National Park Service.

Soldiers moved past Caulk's house during the battle, but it was left unscathed. He raised cows, horses and pigs there until he died in the 1830s, says Hemstock. The house traded hands a number of times during the next century, property records show, until another war shaped its history.

Richard's grandfather, Dutch grain merchant Cornelis van Stolk, was traveling abroad when Nazi Germany invaded the Netherlands in May 1940, says Richard, 72. Rather than return home, Cornelius and his wife remained in the U.S., purchasing the Maryland farm to learn more about American farming.

That same year, Cornelis accepted a royal commission from the Netherlands to stockpile food in preparation for liberation. When Nazi occupation ended in 1945, ships carrying tens of thousands of tons of provisions delivered the food he accumulated, according to the Holland Museum Volunteer Program. Before he died in 1978, he passed the farm on to his three sons. Today, their 14 children share ownership of the corn and soybean-producing farm.
Modern day
The main house is now used as a guesthouse for visiting family, says Richard, who manages the farm and lives in another house on the property.
Historic details

The house has a few quirks. Richard, who stands at 6-foot-5-inches tall, has to duck in some rooms, and some of the staircases are steep and windy. The doorways aren't standard size, so he's had to commission custom wood doors when they needed replacing, he says. "It's sort of like you're living in an antique."
The best part of owning an historic home
"It's just unique, and it's a very welcoming spot," Richard says. "It's got a pleasant, sort of homey feeling."
The hardest part of owning an historic home
"The upkeep always becomes more than you think it will be."
Reason for selling?
Managing a property with 14 co-owners around the world is "too confusing and complicated to continue," Richard says.
Market snapshot

The family is pursuing a conservation easement to protect the house and battlefield. While easements typically diminish land value, "no one is buying this for a housing development," says listing agent Francis Joe Hickman of Cross Street Realtors. The buyer will likely be someone looking to farm and hunt, he says.

Hickman says he expects the property to sell for a premium due to its historic ties. Homes in Kent County sold for about $389,000 in the second quarter, up 8.9% from the same time last year, according to Redfin.
